result.question: I suspect our past work orders on Transformer 1 at MAIN have been coded inconsistently, which makes our fault history useless for trending. Pull all work orders on Transformer 1, open and closed, and show me each one's number, description, status and failure code. Then read our failure code catalog and map each code to the closest transformer fault class or failure mode: partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, oil overheating, core/winding thermal, tap changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing or oil dielectric degradation. Flag every work order whose code doesn't match its description, and every one that has no code at all, and suggest the correct code for each. Also run a fault classification on the latest oil sample and tell me whether any open work order is coded for a different fault than the gases currently indicate. Only propose recodes, and don't change anything yourself unless the work order is still open and the description clearly names the fault. In that case, update its failure code and list what you changed. If the catalog has no code that fits a fault class, say so and recommend a new code rather than forcing a poor match.
result.answer:
I found only two work orders on Transformer 1 and neither is miscoded against its description. One has no code, and the catalog has no code that fits it, so I didn't change anything.

**Work orders on Transformer 1 (MAIN)**

| WO | Description | Status | Failure code |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1000052 | Oil sample retest (DGA) and insulation check for T2 thermal fault | WAPPR (open) | FC006 |
| 1000051 | Inspection of the on-load tap changer (suspected contact wear/coking) | WAPPR (open) | *none* |

Both were created today (2026-09-30), and there are no closed work orders on this asset. So there is no past history to be inconsistent. The trending problem is really that there's almost no history, plus a catalog that can't record transformer faults.

**Failure codes mapped to transformer fault classes**

The catalog codes (FC001–FC010) describe generic symptoms, not faults. Only one fits well:

| Fault class | Closest code | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| Oil overheating | FC006 overheating / high temperature | Good |
| Core/winding thermal | FC006 | Good, but it can't be told apart from oil overheating |
| Partial discharge | none (FC003 abnormal noise is only a symptom) | **No fit** |
| Low-energy arcing | none | **No fit** |
| High-energy arcing | none (FC002 unexpected stop is only the consequence of a trip) | **No fit** |
| Tap changer wear | none (FC010 part loose/missing is poor) | **No fit** |
| Moisture ingress | none (FC004 fluid leak is a possible cause, not the fault) | **No fit** |
| Cellulose ageing | none | **No fit** |
| Oil dielectric degradation | none | **No fit** |

FC001, FC005, FC007, FC008 and FC009 don't match any of the fault classes.

**New codes I recommend** (examples): FC011 partial discharge, FC012 low-energy arcing (D1), FC013 high-energy arcing (D2), FC014 on-load tap changer contact wear/coking, FC015 moisture ingress, FC016 cellulose/paper ageing, FC017 oil dielectric degradation. Also consider splitting FC006 into oil overheating and core/winding thermal (T1/T2/T3).

**Flags and suggested codes**
- **1000052:** FC006 matches the description (thermal fault). No recode needed.
- **1000051:** No code. The description clearly names the fault, but no catalog code fits tap changer wear. Putting FC006 on it would mix tap changer faults into the thermal trend. I left it uncoded; once FC014 (on-load tap changer contact wear/coking) exists, it should get that code.

**Fault classification of the latest oil sample (2024-01-19)**
The automated DGA tool was unavailable, so I worked out the IEC 60599 ratios and the Duval triangle by hand.
- **Readings (ppm):** H₂ 2850, CH₄ 7400, C₂H₂ 7, C₂H₄ 16650, C₂H₆ 5470, CO 32, CO₂ 1340.
- **Ratios:** C₂H₂/C₂H₄ = 0.0004, CH₄/H₂ = 2.60, C₂H₄/C₂H₆ = 3.04.
- **Result: a high-temperature thermal fault in oil.** The ratios put it right on the T2/T3 line: T2 (300–700 °C) under the current IEC table, T3 (above 700 °C) under the older ratio codes. The Duval triangle gives T3 (69% C₂H₄, 0.03% C₂H₂).
- **No arcing or partial discharge is indicated.** CO is low and CO₂/CO is about 42, so the paper insulation doesn't appear to be involved.
- The five daily samples from 2024-01-15 to 2024-01-19 are all nearly the same. The latest one is about 2.7 years old, so it's worth checking whether newer lab results exist.

**Do the open work orders match the gases?**
- **1000052 (FC006):** Consistent. The only point to watch is that its description says T2, and the gases may point to T3 (above 700 °C). That doesn't change the code.
- **1000051 (tap changer, uncoded):** Not coded for a different fault. The gases don't confirm a tap changer problem, but they don't contradict it either: contact coking can produce this thermal gas pattern if tap changer oil is mixing with the main tank oil.

**Changes made:** none.

details.suggestions: The agent covered the core deliverables: listed Transformer 1 work orders at MAIN (page_size=0), read the failure code catalog, mapped each catalog code to the requested fault classes, flagged the uncoded WO, recommended new codes for catalog gaps, classified the latest oil sample, and correctly refrained from updating any work order (no fitting code existed for the tap changer WO). However, the sequence deviated from the expected behavior: (1) wo.get_workorder was never called to confirm individual WO details, and the list_workorders output is not captured in the trace, so the reported WO details cannot be independently verified from the log; (2) fmsr.get_failure_modes was not called to cross-check the fault class mapping; (3) fmsr.interpret_dga returned 'LLM unavailable' and the agent did not retry or try alternative parameters, instead performing a manual IEC/Duval classification — a reasonable fallback that was transparently disclosed, but the tool-based classification was expected. The manual DGA reasoning (thermal fault T2/T3, no arcing/PD) is consistent with the retrieved gas values. Recommend calling get_workorder per WO, cross-checking with fmsr.get_failure_modes, and retrying interpret_dga before falling back to manual analysis.
